name: Meister Eckhart
biography:
Meister Eckhart (circa 1260–1328), born Johannes Eckhart in Hochheim near Frankfurt, stands as the most profound and most controversial Christian mystic of the medieval period and as the supreme Christian reception of Neoplatonic henosis doctrine. A Dominican friar of extraordinary theological training, Eckhart mastered scholastic theology in the tradition of Thomas Aquinas, engaged deeply with the apophatic theology of Pseudo-Dionysius, and articulated a mystical vision of union with God that drew directly from Neoplatonic sources while remaining committed to Christian orthodoxy. Yet this vision proved so radical that it provoked ecclesiastical suspicion and posthumous condemnation.

Eckhart's intellectual formation occurred within the Dominican order, the intellectual elite of medieval Christianity. He studied at the University of Paris, the supreme center of scholastic theology in the thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries. He received his doctorate in theology and rose through the Dominican hierarchy to positions of considerable authority: he served as Prior of Erfurt, as provincial of the Dominican order in Germany, and as Master of Scripture at Paris. His German sermons, preached to lay audiences in the Rhineland, became famous for their profundity and spiritual intensity. Yet these very sermons, with their radical claims about union with God and the annihilation of the self in God, provoked criticism and eventually led to ecclesiastical investigation.

Eckhart's philosophical theology, developed most systematically in his Parisian Questions and in his Sermons and Lectures, represents a comprehensive engagement with Aristotelian scholasticism in the service of a vision of mystical theology that is fundamentally Neoplatonic. The intellectual architecture is scholastic: Eckhart accepts the categories of Aristotelian philosophy and the methods of dialectical reasoning. Yet the spiritual vision he articulates transcends scholasticism: he insists that the ultimate goal of human existence is not philosophical knowledge but mystical union with God, a union that transcends all discursive thought and rational analysis.

The central theme of Eckhart's theology is the radical transcendence and utter simplicity of God. God is not being (esse) in the sense that creatures are beings. Rather, God is the ground of being, the source from which all being flows, yet God is utterly beyond being. In the most distinctive vocabulary of Neoplatonism (via Pseudo-Dionysius), God is beyond being, beyond essence, beyond intellection. God is the Godhead, a term Eckhart uses to denote the divine nature in its absolute transcendence, prior to and beyond the distinction between God the Father, God the Word, and God the Holy Spirit. This insistence on God's radical transcendence is, paradoxically, the foundation for Eckhart's doctrine of mystical union: precisely because God is utterly transcendent and utterly simple, the union of the soul with God transcends all mediation. The soul may be united directly with the Godhead.

Eckhart's doctrine of detachment (Abgeschiedenheit) represents the spiritual correlate of this theological vision. The human soul must detach itself from all particular attachments—to objects, to images, to thoughts, even to images of God. The soul must achieve a perfect emptiness, a poverty of spirit in which it clings to nothing. In this state of radical detachment, the soul is open to receive the Godhead. The soul does not achieve union through its own effort but through allowing itself to be emptied so that God may fill it. This doctrine echoes the apophatic theology of Pseudo-Dionysius: the soul ascends to God through negation, through stripping away all positive content, all images and concepts, until it reaches a state where it knows God by unknowing.

The mystical experience that Eckhart describes goes beyond mere knowledge to a transformative union. In the highest state of mystical contemplation, the distinction between the soul and God dissolves. The soul knows itself in God and God in itself with perfect immediacy. Eckhart uses the language of birth: God is eternally born in the soul; the soul is eternally born in God. This language of mutual birth expresses the reciprocal character of the mystical union. God's self-manifestation in the soul and the soul's return to God are experienced as a single, eternal event. The soul touches the eternal ground of being and experiences itself as participating in God's own self-knowledge.

This mystical vision was grounded in Eckhart's rigorous philosophical theology. He argues that the intellect is the highest faculty of the human soul. In intellectual contemplation, the soul transcends sensory knowledge and even imaginative thought. The intellect, in its actualization, becomes one with its object. When the intellect knows eternal truth, it participates in the eternal knowledge of God. The highest intellection is mystical: the knower, the knowing, and the known become one. This doctrine derives directly from Neoplatonic epistemology but is given Christian interpretation: God as the object of knowledge is recognized as the Godhead, the transcendent source beyond the Trinity.

Eckhart's doctrine of creation represents another point where Neoplatonic and scholastic theology are integrated. Creation is understood as the emanation of all things from the Godhead. Yet God does not create through any act of will or deliberation, which would imply composition in God. Rather, all things flow from God necessarily, as light flows from the sun. God is eternally creative; creation is God's eternal self-manifestation. All beings exist in God, participate in God, are modes of God's being. This bold formulation brought Eckhart dangerously close to pantheism—the doctrine that God and nature are one—and it was precisely such formulations that his critics seized upon.

The practical implications of Eckhart's mystical theology extended to his understanding of Christian life and practice. The highest form of Christian virtue is not active charity in the world but mystical contemplation. Yet Eckhart insists that the contemplative life and the active life are ultimately unified in God. The soul that has achieved mystical union with God is so filled with divine goodness that it overflows in love and service to others. The greatest commandment—to love God with all one's heart, soul, mind, and strength—culminates in mystical union. Yet from this union flows the second commandment, to love one's neighbour as oneself.

Eckhart's use of paradox and apophatic language is remarkably sophisticated. He speaks of knowing through unknowing, of divine darkness, of silence. He employs the language of negation to express truths that cannot be captured in positive predication. This rhetorical strategy, inherited from Pseudo-Dionysius and the Neoplatonic tradition, allows Eckhart to gesture toward truths that transcend discursive language. The reader or hearer is invited to move beyond the words toward a direct experience of the reality they point to. Many of his most powerful sayings are deliberately paradoxical: God alone is truly being, creatures are nothing; the soul must become empty so that God may fill it; the highest knowledge is ignorance; the deepest love is freedom from all personal desire.

The response to Eckhart's theology among his Dominican brothers was complex. Some recognized him as a profound spiritual teacher and a rigorous theologian. Others grew concerned about the apparent contradictions between his mystical language and scholastic precision. The question that troubled them: when Eckhart spoke of the soul becoming God or of the dissolution of the distinction between soul and God, did he mean this literally? If so, did this not deny the essential distinction between Creator and creature? If metaphorically, was the language not dangerously misleading to ordinary believers who might misunderstand?

In 1326, Eckhart was brought before the Inquisition in Avignon to respond to charges of heresy. He composed a lengthy defense of his doctrines, attempting to show that his language, though radical, was consistent with Christian orthodoxy properly understood. He argued that when he spoke of the union of the soul with God, he meant the soul's participation in God's being through knowledge and love. When he spoke of the soul becoming God, he was using the language of mystical theology, not asserting literal transformation. He claimed authority from Pseudo-Dionysius, from Augustine, from the great Christian mystics. The proceedings dragged on; Eckhart died in 1328 before a final judgment was rendered.

Posthumously, Eckhart's condemnation came in 1329. Twenty-eight propositions from his writings were condemned as heretical or suspect of heresy. Yet even this condemnation did not suppress his influence. Eckhart's teachings were transmitted through his students and followers, particularly Heinrich Tauler and Johanne Wesel, who refined and moderated his language while preserving his mystical vision. The tradition of the Rhineland mystics—the Gottesfreunde (friends of God)—carried forward Eckhart's spirituality. The anonymous spiritual treatise Theologia Deutsch, one of the most influential spiritual works of the late medieval period, shows clear influence from Eckhart's doctrines.

Meister Eckhart's philosophy of language and Being represents a distinctive contribution to the history of Neoplatonism within Christianity. He recognized that the Neoplatonic principle of the One, the transcendent and ineffable source of all being, posed particular challenges to Christian theology. How could the Christian insist on God's trinity while maintaining that God is utterly simple and beyond distinction? How could Christian doctrine assert both God's transcendence and the Incarnation, God's entry into human form? Eckhart's response was not to resolve these tensions through logical argumentation (which would merely domesticate the mystery) but to acknowledge them while asserting that they are transcended in mystical experience. The soul, in union with God, knows the Trinity and transcendence together, not as logical contradiction but as paradoxical truth.

The historical reception of Meister Eckhart in the centuries following his death was remarkable. Despite his condemnation, his writings continued to circulate and to influence Christian theology. The Protestant Reformers, particularly Martin Luther, found in Eckhart a precedent for mystical theology and for the critique of mere external religiosity. German philosophical idealism, beginning with Hegel, rediscovered Eckhart as a profound thinker wrestling with the ultimate principles of Being and becoming. The twentieth-century philosopher Martin Heidegger found in Eckhart a medieval precedent for thinking Being beyond traditional metaphysics.

Meister Eckhart's significance in the history of Neoplatonism lies in his demonstration that the Neoplatonic doctrine of henosis—mystical union with the transcendent One—could be brought into profound engagement with Christian trinitarian theology. Though his contemporaries found his formulations troubling and his critics eventually condemned him, Eckhart articulated a vision of Christian mysticism so deep and so rigorous that it remained a permanent possibility within Christian spirituality. Every Christian mystic after Eckhart, whether acknowledging his influence or not, worked in the shadow of his achievement. The insistence that the soul may know God directly, not through images or concepts but in naked encounter; that this knowledge transcends all discursive thought; that it is attained not through the soul's effort but through receptive openness—these Eckhardt doctrines, rooted in Neoplatonic henosis as understood through Pseudo-Dionysius, became permanent features of Christian mystical theology.
